name: PT Yupi Indo Jelly Gum Tbk

frontmatter.title: Yupi Indo Jelly Gum - a strong brand priced for growth it has not delivered
frontmatter.summary: Yupi is a profitable, net-cash gummy and jelly confectioner with a leading domestic brand and a real export franchise, but three years of flat-to-down revenue and a 2026 margin gain that is input-cost relief plus a depreciation change - not pricing power - leave it trading at a rich multiple. We initiate at REDUCE, target Rp1,042 against Rp1,255, a total return of -13.1%. The konglo lens keeps part of the ownership premium, so this is not a deep SELL.
thesis: A genuinely good business on the numbers - gross margin of 34.3%, EBITDA margin of 31.4%, net cash at FY2025 and return on equity of 32.2% - but one that has not grown: revenue was IDR3,135.0bn in FY2023 and IDR2,935.8bn in FY2025 [S7].

The 2026 improvement is an input-cost cycle plus a depreciation change. Nine-month 2026 gross margin rose because raw materials fell faster than net revenue while sales discounts climbed, and the useful lives were extended from 1 January 2026; we fade the modelled margin from 39.2% to 37.5% by FY2030E rather than hold the peak [S6].

The shares discount growth we cannot find in the accounts: at 18.4x our FY2026E EPS of Rp68 and 12.3x EV/EBITDA the market needs about 5.8% a year of additional revenue growth, an implied 8.8% in FY2027E, to justify Rp1,255 on our own DCF [S0].

Ownership, not the business, sets the marginal price: the controller holds 90.0% and the free float is 10.0%, the shares have left the IHSG from 2 November 2026, and a staged remedy is due by 31 March 2027; dilution is a live option alongside a controller sell-down [S14][S16][S12].

Base case is the most likely path, not the most cautious: we value at Rp784 on fundamentals and Rp679 after the liquidity discount, then the konglo lens restores part of the ownership premium to Rp1,042.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Yupi Indo Jelly Gum Tbk with a **REDUCE** rating and a target of Rp1,042, against a last price of Rp1,255: an expected total return of -13.1% including the next twelve months of dividends of Rp48. The call is not that Yupi is a bad company. It is a well-run, cash-generative confectioner with a brand that has been in Indonesian hands for decades, two modern plants and a genuine export business. The call is that the price already pays for a growth and a margin profile the accounts do not show.

The business printed IDR2,935.8bn of revenue, IDR923.2bn of EBITDA and IDR613.1bn of net profit in FY2025, on our restated D&A figure [S7]. That is an EBITDA margin of 31.4% and a net margin of 20.9% - high for a confectioner, and the reason the stock is not cheap on any measure. Our FY2026E numbers are IDR2,918.2bn of revenue and IDR584.1bn of net profit, with EPS of Rp68: revenue is flat and profit is a little below the prior year, because nine months of 2026 already show revenue slightly lower while marketing, staff and professional fees stepped up [S6]. That profit is built on the post-2026 depreciation rates rather than the old ones, and the fourth quarter implied by our full-year figure is in line with the prior-year quarter rather than far below it.

Our variant view has three parts. First, the margin: the 2026 gain came from raw materials falling faster than net revenue while sales discounts and rebates rose, not from price, and part of the reported gain is the depreciation change [S6]. We model the printed margin at 39.2% in FY2026E, fading to 37.5% by FY2030E and 36.2% in the long run. That is above FY2025's 34.3%, but the comparison is not like for like: the useful lives extended from 1 January 2026 cut depreciation inside cost of goods sold, so part of the gap is the change in estimate rather than trading, and on the old lives the modelled margin would be lower [S6]. Second, growth: the company has expanded capacity and says it will push exports, but revenue has been flat to down for three years and the IPO proceeds earmarked for capex were still unspent at the FY2025 report date [S7][S8]. Third, ownership: the free float is 10.0% against a controller holding 90.0%, so the marginal buyer is scarce and the remedy that lifts the float - a placement, a rights issue or an ESOP - can add shares [S12].

The valuation says the same thing from the other direction. Our DCF values the equity at Rp835 a share at a WACC of 11.0%, the multiples cross-checks sit below that at Rp691 on P/E and Rp755 on EV/EBITDA, and the blended value before the liquidity discount is Rp784 [S0]. Asked what the market price of Rp1,255 requires, the reverse DCF answers revenue growth about 5.8% a year higher than we forecast in every year - an implied 8.8% rate for FY2027E against our 3.0%.

Two things stop us from a SELL. The first is that the fundamentals are not deteriorating: net cash, a payout held at about 70.8% of profit with three interim dividends declared in 2026, the third smaller than the second, and a category that still grows with nominal consumption. The second is the konglo lens, which is part of this target rather than an afterthought. On fundamentals the shares are worth Rp679 after the liquidity discount; the lens recognises that a tightly held name with this brand can carry a persistent ownership premium, and in the base case it restores a fraction of the gap, giving Rp1,042. That is a premium of 1.95 times fundamental value today, of which the base case assumes about 0.40 of the log excess closes within twelve months. If the float remedy is clean, the premium survives; if it is dilutive, it does not.

Yupi makes jelly and gummy confectionery, and the product range on its own investor site runs from gummy and jelly pieces through extruded shapes to marshmallow and lollipop [S9]. Production sits in two plants - the original Gunung Putri site in Bogor, West Java, which is also the head office, and the Karanganyar plant in Central Java - and the annual report puts the workforce at 1,442 people at the FY2025 reporting date [S8]. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange on 25 March 2025, which is recent enough that the public market has only a short price history to work with [S8].

The revenue mix is disclosed by geography rather than by product. FY2025 domestic revenue was IDR2,256.9bn and export revenue IDR773.8bn, both gross of discounts, so exports are roughly a quarter of the gross book [S7]. The annual report describes sales through two main channels, traditional trade and modern trade, and describes export operations to a range of countries without naming them [S8]. Customer concentration is the feature that matters for risk: the FY2025 notes show four distributors above the ten-percent disclosure threshold accounting for close to half of revenue, with the largest - PT Tiga Raksa Satria - at 15.0% [S7].

The cost base is agricultural. Raw materials were IDR1,335.3bn of FY2025 cost of goods sold, the great majority of it, and the notes do not split sugar, glucose syrup, gelatin and flavourings apart [S7]. That matters for two reasons: the input basket is partly imported and therefore carries rupiah risk, and the only house deck series that maps onto it is corn, the feedstock for the glucose and starch sweeteners, which is why we give our corn link a partial share of cost of goods sold rather than treating it as a full index [S0].

The group structure is simple and the control is concentrated. PT Confectionery Consumer Products Indonesia holds 90.0% of the shares and the public the rest, with the beneficial owner identified in the exchange's ownership disclosures [S8][S11]. Operations are run by a professional management team under a president director, with a board of commissioners that mixes Singaporean and Indonesian members and includes one independent commissioner [S8]. The strategy management describes is unremarkable and credible: expand production capacity, deepen the distribution network, widen the export footprint and keep launching products [S8]. The open question is not the strategy but the funding of it - the March 2025 IPO raised IDR612.6bn, of which the capital-expenditure and working-capital earmark was still unused a year later [S8].

Competitively, Yupi is a leader in its niche rather than in confectionery as a whole. Its brand is old and widely recognised, its plants hold the food-safety certifications that modern trade and export customers require [S8], and scale in moulding and packaging gives it a cost position that smaller local producers cannot match. Against that, the category has low switching costs, private label is present in modern trade, and imported candy competes on price at the value end. The strongest part of the franchise is the brand-and-distribution combination in the domestic mass market; the weakest is pricing power, which the rising discount line in 2026 exposes [S6].

Confectionery is a mature, impulse-driven category in most emerging markets: volume tracks population and disposable income, while value per unit is held down by the fact that a pack of candy is a small, repeat purchase with many substitutes on the same shelf. Brand owners earn their margin from distribution reach and shelf space rather than from price, which is why the trade terms a company gives its distributors show up so directly in gross margin.

The company's own market read is that the food-and-beverage sector, confectionery included, still has positive prospects on consumer demand at home and abroad, offset by commodity-price and production-cost volatility and by competition that is getting more intense [S8]. That is a fair summary of the industry's structure: a growing nominal category, a cost base the manufacturer does not control, and a competitive set that includes both global brands and a long tail of local producers. We have not found a disclosed market-share figure for Yupi in the filings or the annual report, so we do not put one in the model; the evidence of position is qualitative - brand recognition, plant certifications and the fact that four distributors of national scale carry the product [S7][S8].

The input-cost driver is the clearest quantitative link we can make. Our agri deck has corn at 172.6 a tonne in FY2025, rising to 214.6 in FY2026E and 215.5 by FY2029E, against a spot print of 174.1 [S0]. Sugar and gelatin have no house series, so the model exposes thirty percent of cost of goods sold to corn with a partial pass-through to price; that is a deliberately modest link, not a claim that corn is the whole basket [S0]. The corn path matters because it explains the 2026 margin and does not repeat it: the relief came from raw-material costs falling in the accounts, while the deck has corn about a quarter above its FY2025 average from FY2026 onward and holds it there through the long-run forecast [S0][S6]. We therefore take the 2026 relief once and fade the margin with the deck rather than assume the input windfall persists.

The macro frame is the standard Indonesian one: real GDP growth of 5.3% and consumer inflation of 3.3% in the house deck, with the rupiah at 17,570 to the dollar in FY2026E against 16,448 in FY2025A [S0]. A weaker rupiah cuts both ways for Yupi: it raises the rupiah cost of imported inputs and of any dollar-denominated packaging, and it makes export revenue worth more when translated. With exports at roughly a quarter of the gross book, the net effect is modest but not zero, and it is one reason we do not model margin expansion beyond the input cycle.

Regulation touches the business in three places. Food safety and production certification - the CPPOB good-manufacturing-practice regime the plants are certified under - is a barrier to entry and a compliance cost [S8]. Halal and product registration requirements govern what can be sold and where, and are a precondition for the modern-trade and export channels [S8]. And the exchange's free-float rule is now a governance constraint on the shares themselves, with staged deadlines that the company has told the exchange it will meet [S12]. We treat the first two as part of the moat and the third as a risk to the share count.

Five forces, briefly, since the moat is the point of the section. Supplier power is high and rising on the agricultural inputs, because the basket is commodity-priced and partly imported [S7]. Buyer power is high and concentrated, with the top distributors at 15.0% and close to half of revenue across four names, and with modern-trade chains able to delist a slow seller [S7]. The threat of new entrants is moderate: the brand and the certified plants are hard to replicate at scale, but private label and imports do not need either. Substitutes are plentiful - every other snack on the shelf - and rivalry is intense, which is exactly what a rising discount line signals [S6]. The moat is therefore real but narrow: distribution and brand inside Indonesia, no pricing power, and a customer base that can extract terms.

The external influences we watch are the input complex, the rupiah, the health-and-sugar agenda that governments in the region keep circling, and the domestic consumer's willingness to pay for branded impulse purchases when real incomes are squeezed [S8]. None of these is in crisis for Yupi today; the point is that none of them supports a premium multiple either.

The history is a flat business with a changing cost line. Revenue was IDR2,873.1bn in FY2022, IDR3,135.0bn in FY2023, IDR3,042.8bn in FY2024 and IDR2,935.8bn in FY2025, a change of -3.5% in the last year [S7]. Net profit held up better than revenue at IDR613.1bn because the gross margin improved and other income helped, but the direction is clear: this is not a growth franchise on the last three years' evidence [S7]. Our FY2026E revenue of IDR2,918.2bn continues that pattern, because nine-month 2026 revenue of IDR2,237.3bn was slightly below the same period a year earlier and gross billings were flat before discounts rose [S6].

The margin story needs care, and it is where the data pack is wrong. The pack carries FY2025 D&A of a few billion rupiah; the fixed-asset note allocates IDR154.6bn of depreciation in FY2025 and IDR139.6bn in FY2024 [S7]. That is roughly a twentieth of the real charge, and because the template rebuilds EBITDA as EBIT plus D&A, leaving it uncorrected would have understated EBITDA and depressed every EBITDA multiple in this report. We restate D&A, EBIT and parent net profit from the LK for both years, which is why the EBITDA line in the table steps up in FY2024 - the step is a correction, not a change in the business [S7]. FY2025 EBITDA on the restated basis is IDR923.2bn, a margin of 31.4%.

The second accounting item is a change in estimate, and it runs the other way. From 1 January 2026 the company extended the useful lives of machinery from eight to thirty years and of buildings from twenty to thirty years, a prospective change that cut nine-month depreciation by IDR74.5bn and left total depreciation at IDR41.6bn against IDR154.6bn for the whole of FY2025 [S6]. Because depreciation is charged inside cost of goods sold and within general and administrative expense, the change lifts reported gross profit and operating profit as well as the profit line; it also shrinks the depreciation add-back that turns EBIT into EBITDA. Our model carries both effects. The printed margin is taken from the accounts, and the D&A line is rebuilt on the new lives at IDR56.9bn for FY2026E on revenue of IDR2,918.2bn, against a charge two and a half times that size in FY2025 [S6][S7]. The ratio then creeps up as the capex programme adds assets, partly offset by the IDR454.6bn of gross fixed assets that are already fully depreciated and still in use [S6].

Put the two margins together and the accounting change becomes visible. FY2026E EBIT margin is 26.8% against 26.2% in FY2025A - flat - while the EBITDA margin falls from 31.4% to 28.8% [S0]. EBITDA is struck before depreciation, so the useful-life change cannot move it: it lifts EBIT by the smaller charge inside cost of goods sold and G&A and cuts the depreciation add-back by the same amount, which is exactly why the EBIT margin reads flat while the EBITDA margin falls. The EBITDA decline itself is the cost base the nine-month accounts actually show: gross profit of IDR876.0bn against IDR748.8bn a year earlier on slightly lower revenue, but SG&A net of other operating income at 12.4% of revenue against a much lower ratio a year earlier. Strip the lower depreciation charge out of both lines and the cost step still exceeds the gross-profit gain, which is what the EBITDA line measures [S6]. FY2026E is anchored on that latest actual, which is what the base-case card asks for: no margin haircut, no price give-away and no extra cost is embedded in the model.

On the cost side, raw materials were IDR1,335.3bn of cost of goods sold in FY2025, and the 2026 improvement took the printed gross margin to 39.2% from 34.3% in FY2025 because that line fell faster than net revenue [S6][S7]. The nine-month accounts show the mechanism directly: gross profit of IDR876.0bn on revenue of IDR2,237.3bn, a margin well above the same period a year earlier [S6]. What gives part of it back is trade terms: sales discounts and rebates rose to IDR88.9bn in the first nine months of 2026, from a materially lower base a year earlier [S6]. The agri deck then keeps corn above its FY2025 average for the rest of the horizon [S0], so we fade the printed margin to 37.5% by FY2030E and 36.2% across the ten-year horizon rather than hold the peak. Operating costs are the other 2026 change: selling, general and administrative expense net of other operating income ran at 12.4% of revenue in the nine months against a much lower ratio a year earlier, with marketing and promotion, professional fees and salaries all stepping up [S6]. We treat the marketing step as structural and fade the professional-fee line, taking the ratio to 11.5% by FY2030E [S6].

Cash flow and capital intensity are the part of the equity story we like. FY2025 operating cash generation comfortably covered net profit, and the balance sheet was already in net cash: the engine's net-debt line is IDR-93bn, negative because cash of IDR868bn exceeds borrowing [S7]. The borrowing is drawn under syndicated facilities in the financing-liabilities note of the interim accounts, with a revolving tranche alongside, not a bond maturity wall [S6]. Capex was only IDR62.4bn, about 2.1% of revenue, against D&A of IDR154.6bn: a company that has finished a plant build and is under-investing relative to its depreciation charge [S7]. That cannot persist, and the IPO proceeds were earmarked for capex and working capital [S8]; we model capex rising to 6.0% of revenue in FY2027E and 5.5% by FY2030E, which deploys part of that programme without assuming the whole amount is spent inside the forecast [S8].

Working capital is material relative to revenue and is the bridge between profit and cash. FY2025 operating working capital was IDR266.1bn; the filing shows receivables and inventories of comparable size against payables, and we hold operating working capital at 9.0% of revenue through the forecast [S7]. The FY2025 cash flow benefited from a working-capital release, which is why free cash flow of IDR809.8bn exceeded net profit by a wide margin while still sitting below EBITDA; we do not capitalise that release into the long run [S7].

The balance sheet we anchor on is the 30 September 2026 accounts, not the June quarter the data pack carries. At that date cash was IDR833.8bn against total bank loan and lease liabilities of IDR771.0bn, so the company was still in net cash after paying two interim dividends of IDR287.0bn during the year, and equity stood at IDR1,721.6bn [S6]. The distinction matters: the long-term bank-loan line alone understates total debt because current maturities sit in short-term borrowings and a lease liability sits alongside them, so we take the total from the financing-liabilities note, which reconciles opening and closing debt [S6]. Leverage is not a risk in this name; the risk is that the cash is returned rather than deployed, which is what the 2026 dividend record shows [S2][S6].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly to a fault. FY2025 cash dividends paid were IDR1,900.0bn, but that is not a run-rate and not a pre-IPO extraction: the equity note shows the FY2024 final approved at the AGMS of 25 June 2025 plus an interim from retained earnings at 30 September 2025 approved on 24 November 2025, both paid pro rata to every holder after the March 2025 listing [S7]. The 2026 record is the better guide. Three interims have been declared - IDR141.6bn from retained earnings at 31 March 2026 and paid in May, IDR145.4bn from retained earnings at 30 June 2026 and paid in September, and the IDR126.8bn interim declared on 5 November 2026 and payable on 26 November 2026 [S6][S2]. They set a payout of 70.8% against our FY2026E profit, and we hold that rate thereafter, which leaves the growth capex to be funded from the IPO proceeds rather than from retained cash [S7][S8].

Earnings quality, on the method card's screens. Accruals are not a concern: operating cash flow has tracked or exceeded net profit, helped by the working-capital release, and the cash conversion trend is stable rather than deteriorating [S7]. There is no receivables-outrunning-revenue flag, no inventory build against falling cost of sales, and no sign of capitalised development or borrowing costs creeping into the balance sheet [S7]. Two accounting items did distort the reported record. The first was the data pack's D&A, which we fixed from the filing rather than modelled around [S7]. The second is the change in useful lives from 1 January 2026, which cut nine-month depreciation by IDR74.5bn. That is a real, disclosed, prospective change in estimate rather than an error, but it flatters the year-on-year margin comparison and lowers the quality of the earnings base a buyer of the shares is capitalising [S6]. We classify it as optics-class: aggressive toward anyone comparing 2026 with 2025 without reading the note, but fully disclosed and auditable. On the IDX regime screens we found no special notation and no special-monitoring-board status in the FY2025 report or the 2026 interim accounts [S7][S6]. Related-party flows are not material to revenue: the notes show the ordinary key-management and affiliate balances rather than sales or purchases of substance [S7]. The structure flags are the ones that matter, and they are disclosed rather than hidden: a controller with 90.0%, a free float of 10.0%, four possible dilution routes to fix it, and a dividend policy that returns most of the profit [S7][S12]. We classify those as optics-class too - aggressive toward minority holders but disclosed - and they are the basis of our company-specific premium in the cost of equity, not of a manipulation call.

A branded consumer staple with stable cash generation, modest maintenance capex and a simple balance sheet is the natural home for a discounted cash flow. We weight the DCF at sixty percent, the P/E cross-check at thirty and EV/EBITDA at ten, which is the house set for this industry and reflects the fact that the DCF is the only method that prices the margin fade and the capex normalisation explicitly [S0]. Multiples are a sanity check on what the market is paying, not the value itself.

The cost of capital build is conventional and lands inside the house band, but it only reproduces if the default spread is handled explicitly, so we write it out. The build starts from the ten-year government bond yield of 7.45%, which is not a risk-free rate: because the rupiah sovereign carries default risk, the 1.62% default spread is deducted from it, and the local risk-free rate that enters the formula is 7.45% less 1.62%. To that we add the re-levered beta times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.23% and the Indonesia country premium of 2.46%, plus a 0.50% company-specific premium for the single-category exposure, the distributor concentration, the float and the undecided exit of the private-equity controller [S7][S12]. The unlevered beta of 0.70 re-levers to 0.74 at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.07. Arithmetically, cost of equity = (7.45% - 1.62%) + 0.74 x (4.23% + 2.46%) + 0.50% = 11.28%. The pre-tax debt cost of 9.45% is likewise taken from the house macro build, risk-free plus the corporate debt spread, and is deliberately not the 7.8% the company actually pays on its facility; with a 93.3% equity weight, a 6.7% debt weight and the 22.0% statutory rate, WACC = 93.3% x 11.28% + 6.7% x 9.45% taxed at 22.0% = 11.01%, inside the house band. The company's own borrowing cost is used only to run the forecast interest line, where the nine-month run-rate of finance costs on the drawn balance is the right number. We do not use a higher rate to express our caution: caution belongs in the scenarios, and a WACC outside the band would be a number looking for a conclusion [S0].

The DCF values the equity at Rp835 a share, an enterprise value of IDR7,198bn, with 51.3% of the value in the terminal period - high, but normal for a company growing in the low single digits with a 11.0% discount rate. Three judgements drive it: the printed margin fade from 39.2% to 37.5% and then 36.2% as the corn deck holds about a quarter above its FY2025 average and the sales-discount line keeps rising, the revenue path from 3.0% to 4.0%, and the operating-cost ratio settling at 11.5% of revenue against a capex programme of 6.0% of revenue [S6]. Terminal growth is 4.0%, below nominal GDP and below our explicit years, because the category is mature and the company's own record is flat [S7].

The multiple-survival test and the growth identity are the two checks that keep a terminal value honest, and both are worth stating because 51.3% of the DCF sits in the terminal period. On the multiple, the terminal value capitalises FY2035E EBITDA of IDR1,109.1bn at an implied exit EV/EBITDA of almost nine times and FY2035E EBIT of IDR1,016.6bn at about nine and a half times. That is about a quarter above the 7.1x peer-median entry multiple we apply in the cross-check, and far below the 12.3x the current price implies on FY2026E earnings. So the DCF does assume some multiple expansion relative to the entry multiple, and we say so rather than leave it buried in the terminal value. We accept it for three reasons and flag one limit. The exit multiple is not a re-rating input but the arithmetic result of capitalising a terminal cash flow that still grows at 4.0% on a business earning an incremental return above its cost of capital; the entry multiple is a peer median set by de-rated comparables and applied to a trailing, better year; and the implied exit sits far below what the market pays today, so the DCF is not validating the current price. The limit is the one the house de-rating base rate warns about: a terminal multiple above today's peer median is exactly what premium consumer names have not been able to hold, which is why every other judgement in the model leans the other way and why we would rather be accused of understating this DCF than of capitalising a re-rating [S0][S7].

Growth in the terminal period is manufactured, not declared, and the identity is g = reinvestment rate x return on incremental capital. On the model's own terminal year, FY2035E free cash flow of IDR647.0bn is about four fifths of NOPAT (FY2035E EBIT of IDR1,016.6bn taxed at 22.0%), so the reinvestment rate behind the 4.0% terminal growth is about a fifth of NOPAT and the implied return on incremental capital is about a fifth - roughly twice the 11.0% discount rate. That is a fade, not a franchise assumption: return on equity is already down to 21.3% in the terminal year from 32.2% in FY2025, and the incremental return we imply is below the return the business earns on its capital today. The same identity is why we do not close the gap to the market by lifting growth: the 8.8% FY2027E growth the price requires would need a far higher reinvestment rate, or a far higher incremental return, than a mature confectioner has shown [S7][S8].

The two cross-checks sit below the DCF, and we are comfortable with the direction rather than the size. Both are applied to the same year, and that year is FY2025A rather than a forecast: because we restate revenue, operating profit and parent net profit from the LK, the engine replaces the pack's trailing measure with the last audited actual, so the P/E of 9.6x capitalises FY2025A earnings of IDR613.1bn and the EV/EBITDA of 7.1x capitalises FY2025A EBITDA of IDR923.2bn [S0]. That gives Rp691 and Rp755 a share, -17.3% and -9.6% against the DCF. The weakness of that construction is that the trailing year is also the better one: FY2026E EPS is Rp68 against Rp72, so on today's price the forward multiples are 18.4x and 17.7x on P/E and 12.3x on EV/EBITDA - the shares are not cheap on either year. The direction of the gap is expected: the multiples capitalise a single year, while the DCF sees the margin fade and the capex step in the later years. We take the gap as evidence that the market's current multiple needs earnings growth the accounts do not show, not as a reason to cut the DCF [S0].

The probability-weighted value across the three business scenarios is Rp849 a share once each is rolled forward twelve months, from a present value today of Rp784. We apply a liquidity discount of 20.0% for the 10.0% free float and an average daily traded value of IDR116.4m, which is small for an institutional position; that gives a fundamental value of Rp679 [S0][S12]. This is what an owner of the whole company could rationally pay, and it is well below the market price.

The konglo lens is what reconciles that with our target, and it is not a fudge. The shares trade at 1.95 times our fundamental value per share, and the regime work says that for a company held this tightly - 90.0% by one shareholder, 99.9% of the stock accounted for under the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration method - the marginal price is set by scarcity of float rather than by fundamentals [S11]. Mechanically the target is the fundamental value grossed up by the premium factor, price over fundamental value raised to one minus the share of the gap that closes within twelve months. The share is set by regime scenario, and it is the share of the log gap that CLOSES, not the share of the premium kept: about 0.80 in the bear case, 0.40 in the base case, and a small negative allowance in the bull case (-0.05) where the register widens and the premium re-widens slightly rather than closing [S0][S12].

The regime that sets those shares is live, not historic. The exchange maintains a list of its most concentrated issuers as of 26 October 2026, and those names already sit outside the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 [S13][S14]; MSCI opened a consultation on moving Indonesia to standalone status on 15 October 2026, with a final decision due by the end of June 2027 and index increases frozen in the meantime [S15]; and the amended listing rule requires the float to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full minimum a year later [S16]. The lens carries two additive adjustments for exactly those facts - one for the high-shareholding status, one for the deadline window - rather than a sentiment call on the stock. In the base case the gross-up takes the fundamental value to Rp1,012, and the probability-weighted result across the three lens scenarios is our target of Rp1,042.

Asked what the price implies, the reverse DCF answers revenue growth. Holding our margins and cost of capital, Rp1,255 requires 5.8% of additional revenue growth in every year on top of our forecast, which takes FY2027E growth from our 3.0% to an implied 8.8% [S0]. That is not an absurd number for a consumer company in a growing economy - which is precisely why the call is REDUCE and not SELL - but it is growth the last three years of accounts do not support, and it has to be delivered while absorbing a margin that fades and a capex programme that restarts [S7][S8].

The downside risks, ranked by expected damage. First, margin give-back: the gross margin of 39.2% we model for FY2026E depends on input costs staying near deck levels, and the trade-discount line is already rising, so a rebound in corn and sugar with no price increase could cost a couple of points of margin - likelihood medium, impact high [S6]. Second, revenue stagnation: three years of flat-to-down revenue make our 3.0% recovery a forecast rather than an extrapolation, and cheaper local and imported candy can take share at the value end - likelihood medium-high, impact medium [S7]. Third, customer concentration: the four largest distributors carry close to half of revenue [S7], so a change in terms with one of them moves the P&L faster than any consumer trend.

Fourth, the float overhang and the index flows it has already triggered. With 10.0% free float against a 90.0% controller, the remedy has to add 2.5% of float by 31 March 2027 and take it to the full minimum by 31 March 2028, and the company has told the exchange that the route could be a controller sell-down, a private placement without pre-emptive rights, a rights issue or an ESOP [S16][S12]. The dilution arithmetic is easy to state and hard to model: a placement that fills the gap at the market price is close to neutral in value per share, the same placement at a discount transfers value from existing holders, and a rights issue at a discount does the same unless every holder follows. At today's price a gap-filling placement adds about 2.5% of the share count and dilutes existing holders by roughly that fraction of book and earnings; the same money raised at our fundamental value takes about 1.9 times as many shares, which is the cost of doing it at the wrong price. That is why the dilution route is carried here, quantitatively, as a risk rather than as a shocked line inside the bear case: the house scenario law allows four mirrored drivers, and a share count cannot be shocked on its own without its proceeds, because a placement at the market price brings cash in with the shares and is close to neutral in value per share - only a placement at a discount to value transfers value from existing holders, and the size of that transfer depends on a discount nobody has announced. The bear value of Rp649 is therefore struck on the 8,544m shares in issue today; what the bear does carry is the higher required return the overhang imposes, through the WACC shock, and the bull case is a clean controller sell-down, which widens the register without adding shares [S0][S12]. The flow side is already in the price. The stock left the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026, it sits on the exchange's concentration list, and MSCI has frozen index increases for Indonesian names while it consults on standalone status, with a decision due by the end of June 2027 [S14][S13][S15]. Each of those removes a class of buyer rather than a unit of earnings, which is exactly the mechanism the konglo lens is built to hold. Fifth, currency: a rupiah at 17,570 against 16,448 raises imported input costs even as it helps export revenue [S0]. Sixth, governance and liquidity: a small float and a single controlling shareholder mean the minority holder has little influence over capital allocation, and the dividend record shows a preference for returning cash over reinvesting it [S7][S2].

The scenarios shock the same four drivers in mirror image, which is the house rule: revenue growth by two points either way, gross margin by one and a half points, operating costs by one point and the WACC by one point, with the base at a half and the two tails at a quarter each [S0]. The bear case puts the value at Rp649 (25.0% probability), the base at Rp824 (50.0%) and the bull at Rp1,099 (25.0%) [S0]. The bear narrative is a cyclical margin that gives back the 2026 gain while discounts keep rising and growth stalls; the bull is a margin that holds as costs stay soft, capacity and exports lift volume, and a clean controller sell-down removes the overhang.

The konglo lens changes the shape of those outcomes rather than only the level. In the bear case 0.80 of the log premium closes and the value is Rp776; in the base case 0.40 closes and the value is Rp1,012; in the bull case the register widens, the lens lets the premium re-widen rather than close and the value is Rp1,366 [S0][S12]. Note the asymmetry that is not ours to choose: the premium has far more room to compress than to widen, so the distribution of outcomes is skewed to the downside relative to a name where the market price is at fundamental value. That is the honest shape of a konglo holding, and it is why the target sits below the price even with a base case that keeps part of the premium.

The bull case is not a hope case, and it is worth stating what it rests on. The balance sheet carried IDR833.8bn of cash against IDR771.0bn of debt at the last report, IDR596.7bn of IPO proceeds is still available to fund the capex that would lift volume, the depreciation change contributes IDR74.5bn of relief to the nine-month profit line and keeps the charge low for years, and a clean sell-down adds float without adding shares [S6][S7][S8]. Those are facts about the balance sheet and the notes rather than a forecast of better trading: on them the bull business case is worth Rp1,037 a share in present-value terms against Rp784 for the base, which is why the bull carries a quarter weight rather than a token one.

The dated calendar that will test this view: the dividend payment on 26 November 2026, the FY2026 audited accounts and the first float step both due by 31 March 2027, the close of MSCI's consultation feedback on 30 April 2027 and its decision by the end of June 2027, and the second float step by 31 March 2028 [S2][S16][S15].

The signposts that would change our view, in order of importance: a clean, non-dilutive sale of controller stock that takes the float above the first threshold without new shares; two consecutive quarters of positive volume-led revenue growth at a stable gross margin; a capex programme that is actually deployed and shows up in volume rather than in the depreciation line; and evidence that the higher marketing spend is buying share rather than defending it [S12][S6]. Any of the first two would move us toward ADD; a dilutive placement at a discount would move us toward SELL.

Yupi is a konglo name in the house sense: a listed company whose shares are held overwhelmingly by one vehicle, with a public float far below the exchange's requirement. PT Confectionery Consumer Products Indonesia owns 90.0% of the shares and the public the remainder, and the exchange's ownership disclosure identifies the beneficial owner behind the controller [S8][S11]. The public register is thin in every sense: 3,610 public single investor identifications, and 99.9% of the stock accounted for by the top holders under the high-shareholding-concentration methodology [S11]. That is the definition of a float that cannot absorb institutional size, and it is why we apply a liquidity discount on top of the DCF rather than pretending the shares are freely traded. The exchange has since formalised the status in its own list, where Yupi appears on the register maintained at 26 October 2026, and the names on that list were taken out of the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 [S13][S14]. MSCI has separately frozen index increases for Indonesian securities and opened a consultation on moving the market to standalone status, with feedback running to the end of April 2027 and a decision due by the end of June 2027 [S15].

The free-float rule is the live governance issue. At 31 August 2026 the free float was 10.0%, and under the amended listing rule the company has a transition to 12.5% by 31 March 2027 - about 4.7 months away - and the full minimum by 31 March 2028 [S12]. That is a near-term deadline, not a distant one, which is why the dilution route is a stated risk in the risks section rather than a footnote. Management told the exchange in September 2026 that the constraint is technical and commercial - mechanism, timing and the right investors - and that it is evaluating four routes: a partial divestment by the controller, a private placement without pre-emptive rights, a rights issue and an ESOP [S12]. No scheme had been chosen. We read that as a genuine option set rather than a plan, and we hold dilution out of the scenario values because the cleanest route - a controller sell-down - is also the one that serves the minority best.

Related-party dealings are limited in the accounts: the FY2025 notes do not show material sales to or purchases from affiliates, and the balance-sheet related-party balances are ordinary [S7]. The governance flag is the cash-return policy instead. IDR1,900.0bn of dividends were paid during FY2025, which the equity note shows to be the FY2024 final approved at the AGMS after the listing plus an interim from retained earnings at 30 September 2025, both paid pro rata to every holder rather than extracted before the IPO [S7]. The controller took the great majority of the cash because it owns 90.0% of the shares, and that is the governance point: the minority's dividend is set by a holder who receives most of it [S11]. Since listing the record has been regular - three interims through 2026 culminating in the IDR126.8bn declared on 5 November 2026 and payable on 26 November 2026 - and the stated policy is discretionary, tied to cash position, investment plans and prospects rather than to a fixed ratio [S2][S9].

On the board and audit, the annual report shows a commissioner set that mixes Indonesian and Singaporean members with one independent commissioner, and the financial statements carry an unmodified audit opinion from the company's auditors [S8]. We found no disclosure of pledged controller shares in the annual report, and no special notation or monitoring-board status attached to the listing [S8][S7]. Those are the boxes that matter for an IDX small cap and they are clean; the concentration of control is a disclosed feature of the structure, not a hidden one.

ESG exposures are the ordinary ones for a confectioner. Food safety and manufacturing certification are the material social issues and the plants hold the CPPOB certification the regime requires [S8]. Sugar content and packaging are the environmental and health issues that the category faces everywhere; the annual report treats sustainability as part of the strategy without quantifying targets we can model [S8]. Labour is not a flagged risk: the workforce is modest and domestic, and no labour dispute is disclosed [S8]. We do not apply an ESG discount, but we note that a single-category confectioner is more exposed than a diversified food company to a shift in health regulation or consumer sentiment against sugar.

The dated catalysts are the dividend payment on 26 November 2026, the FY2026 audited accounts and the first free-float step both due by 31 March 2027, MSCI's standalone decision by the end of June 2027, and the second float deadline on 31 March 2028 [S2][S16][S15]. The IHSG exclusion is already behind us: the shares left the index calculation on 2 November 2026, so that flow is in the price rather than ahead of it [S14]. The dividend is a signal of cash confidence rather than a valuation event; the accounts are the real test, because they will show whether the gross-margin gain survived the input cycle and whether the higher marketing spend bought volume [S6]. The float step is the event that can change the share count and therefore the per-share value, and it is the one we will not be able to model until a scheme is announced [S12].

Between updates we monitor four KPIs. Revenue growth against our -0.6% for FY2026E, with the split between domestic and export so we can see whether the export push is real [S7]. Gross margin against our 39.2%, and specifically the sales discount and rebate line, which is where pricing pressure shows first [S6]. Operating expense as a share of revenue against our 12.4%, watching whether the professional-fee step fades as we assume, plus the depreciation note, because the useful-life change is the one accounting item that can flatter a quarter [S6]. And the free-float file: any exchange announcement, shareholder disclosure or corporate action that changes the share count or the register [S12][S16].

We also watch the cash-return line and the capex line together. A company that keeps paying interims while leaving its IPO capex earmark unspent is telling you where its capital allocation priorities lie, and the mix will decide whether the DCF's capex normalisation is right or whether the cash goes out of the door instead [S8][S2]. The next scheduled review is the FY2026 results, when both questions get a data point.

bear.narrative: The 2026 gross-margin gain proves cyclical: input costs rebound while trade discounts keep rising, so the margin gives back one and a half points; the marketing and staff step does not reverse and revenue growth stalls two points below base as domestic share slips to cheaper local and imported candy. The free-float deadline still hangs over the register and the market keeps charging a higher required return for the float and concentration overhang. No share issue is modelled: a placement adds its proceeds with its shares and only transfers value if it is priced at a discount, which is not yet knowable, so the dilution route is carried as a risk in section 5 rather than as a shock.

bull.narrative: The gross-margin gain holds as raw-material costs stay soft and the new Karanganyar capacity and export push lift volume, with the professional-fee line fading faster than we model. The free-float remedy is a clean controller sell-down that widens the register without dilution, removing the concentration overhang and narrowing the required return.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -0.6%: nine-month 2026 revenue was Rp2,237.3bn, 0.8% below the same period of 2025, and gross billings were flat (+0.5%) before sales discounts and rebates rose from Rp59.6bn to Rp88.9bn [S6]. From FY2027E we use +3% then +4%, which is below nominal GDP in the house macro deck and below the confectionery category's nominal growth: management states it will expand production capacity and export markets, and the March-2025 IPO proceeds of Rp596.73bn were earmarked for capex and working capital and were still unused at the FY2025 report date [S8], but the last three years show revenue flat to down (FY2023 Rp3,135.0bn, FY2024 Rp3,042.8bn, FY2025 Rp2,935.8bn), so we do not underwrite a return to high growth [S7].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The convention follows the house MYOR precedent: the values below are set so that the margin the model PRINTS, after the corn link lifts cost of goods sold by about 3.3% on the deck's FY2026 forecast, is the margin we intend. Modelled FY2026E is 39.2%, the nine-month 2026 actual (gross profit Rp876.0bn on revenue Rp2,237.3bn) against 33.2% a year earlier, because raw-material costs fell faster than net revenue [S6]. We then fade the modelled margin to 37.5% by FY2030E and 36.2% by FY2035E - about three points across the horizon, not the five points of the draft - because two sourced pressures erode part of the gain: sales discounts and rebates rose to Rp88.9bn in 9M26 from Rp59.6bn [S6], and the agri deck has corn 24% above its FY2025 average from FY2026 to FY2028 [S0]. We do not fade back to the FY2025 reported margin: the input relief is in the accounts and the base case holds costs at the last actual.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Sugar, glucose syrup and starch-based sweeteners are the bulk of raw materials (Rp1,335.3bn, 69% of COGS in FY2025) but the annual report does not split them out [S7]. We expose 30% of COGS to the corn series as a partial proxy for the glucose/starch complex, not as a full input index; gelatin, flavourings and packaging are outside the deck.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 55% pass-through: list prices move with a lag and the rising sales-discount line (Rp88.9bn in 9M26 from Rp59.6bn) shows that part of any cost movement is absorbed in trade terms rather than passed to consumers [S6].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 12.36%: nine-month 2026 SG&A net of other operating income was 12.36% of revenue (selling Rp145.5bn, G&A Rp135.0bn, other operating expenses Rp26.2bn, other operating income Rp30.2bn) versus 6.7% in 9M25 [S6]; with nine months of the year reported we hold that ratio for FY2026E rather than assume a fourth-quarter relief. The step is real and sourced: marketing and promotion rose to Rp62.9bn from Rp33.0bn, professional fees to Rp32.2bn from Rp1.9bn, and G&A salaries to Rp95.1bn from Rp58.8bn [S6]. We fade to 11.5% by FY2028E as the professional-fee line (which looks transaction-related) normalises, and hold there; the marketing step is treated as structural.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt on the post-1 January 2026 rates. The company extended machinery and building lives from 8 and 20 years to 30 years from 1 January 2026, which cut nine-month 2026 depreciation by Rp74.49bn: total depreciation fell to Rp41.58bn (COGS Rp37.88bn, G&A Rp2.58bn, selling Rp1.12bn) from Rp116.93bn in 9M25 [S6]. Annualised on Q4 at the same run-rate that is about Rp55bn, or 1.9% of FY2026E revenue, against 5.27% in FY2025 (restated depreciation of Rp154.63bn) [S7]. The ratio then creeps up because the capex programme adds assets: on the modelled capex, additions at 30-year lives add roughly Rp6bn of depreciation a year, partly offset by the Rp454.59bn of gross fixed assets that are already fully depreciated and still in use, which charge nothing [S6]. Holding the old 5.0% would have added back depreciation the P&L no longer charges.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was only Rp62.4bn, 2.1% of revenue, against D&A of Rp154.6bn [S7]: that cannot persist. The annual report states the Rp596.73bn IPO proceeds were earmarked for capital expenditure and working capital and were unused at the FY2025 report date [S8]. We model 3.5% of revenue in FY2026E then 6.0-6.5%, roughly D&A plus a growth layer, which deploys about Rp175bn a year of that programme; we do not assume the full Rp596.73bn is spent inside the five explicit years.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital on the engine line was Rp266.1bn, 9.1% of revenue (current assets less cash, minus current liabilities less current debt) [S0]; the filing shows receivables Rp395.4bn and inventories Rp366.1bn against payables Rp349.7bn [S7]. We hold 9.0%.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 21.8%: FY2025 income tax of Rp170.7bn on pre-tax profit of Rp783.8bn [S7]. The statutory rate is 22% (Law 7/2021); the small gap is permanent differences.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 7.8% on the drawn facility, which is the rate the forecast interest line uses: nine-month 2026 finance costs were Rp45.03bn on bank debt of Rp770.31bn, annualised [S6]. This is NOT the rate in the WACC: the discount rate takes its debt cost from the house macro build (risk-free plus the corporate debt spread, which shows as val.coc.kd_pre_tax), because the WACC must be a market rate rather than the company's own borrowing. The FY2025 full-year ratio (Rp26.6bn) is not comparable because the Rp793.2bn DBS syndicated facility was drawn during 2025 [S7][S6].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 3.7% annualised: nine-month 2026 finance income of Rp23.9bn on opening cash of Rp867.8bn [S6]. The FY2025 ratio (9.0%) includes interest on the IPO proceeds before they were deployed.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the net bank loan fell from Rp773.55bn at end-2025 to Rp770.31bn at 30 September 2026 and dividends are funded from operating cash flow [S6]. The DBS Facility A gives Rp1,304.0bn of committed headroom plus a Rp494.5bn undrawn revolving facility, and no new drawing is disclosed [S6].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: -Rp8bn a year: the final tax on finance income (20%) is deducted below operating profit in the LK - Rp10.2bn in FY2025 and Rp4.8bn in 9M26 - and is not captured by the income-tax line [S6, S7]. Small and held flat.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Effectively zero: non-controlling interests are Rp0.17bn of balance-sheet equity and the minority share of profit was a negative Rp3.6m in FY2025 [S7].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 70.8%: three FY2026 interims have been declared - Rp141.62bn from retained earnings at 31 March 2026 (approved 4 May, paid 20 May) [S6], Rp145.38bn from retained earnings at 30 June 2026 (approved 18 August, paid 2 September) [S6] and Rp126.75bn (Rp14.83 a share) declared 5 November and payable 26 November 2026 [S2] - Rp413.75bn in total, which is 70.8% of our FY2026E net profit of Rp584.1bn. That is the declared rate, not an assumed policy. The FY2025 total of Rp1,900.0bn is not a run-rate: note 16 shows it was the FY2024 final approved at the AGMS of 25 June 2025 plus an interim from retained earnings at 30 September 2025 approved on 24 November 2025, both paid pro rata to every holder after the 25 March 2025 IPO [S7].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero in every scenario: 8,544.49m shares in issue with no buyback or issuance announced [S7]. The free-float remedy could involve a private placement, rights issue or ESOP [S12], but a share count cannot be shocked without its proceeds - a placement at the market price adds cash with the shares and is close to neutral in value per share, and only a discount to value transfers value from holders. The dilution path is therefore carried as a quantified risk in section 5, not as a scenario shock.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%: below the house macro deck's 5.29% real GDP growth for Indonesia and well below nominal GDP (real plus 3.3% CPI), and below our explicit forecast growth; it reflects a mature confectionery category rather than a premium growth franchise.

challenges.challenge: The report and assumptions call the Rp1,900.0bn FY2025 dividend a pre-IPO distribution to the then-owner (assumptions say roughly Rp1,600bn), but S7 note 16 says the two 2025 distributions were the FY2024 final approved at the AGMS of 25 June 2025 and an interim from 30 September 2025 retained earnings approved 24 November 2025 - both after the 25 March 2025 IPO and paid pro rata to all holders. The pre-IPO cash extraction inference is unsupported by its own source.
challenges.answer: Restated the 2025 dividend from the equity note: the FY2024 final approved at the AGMS of 25 June 2025 plus an interim from 30 September 2025 retained earnings approved 24 November 2025, both after the 25 March 2025 listing and paid pro rata to every holder [S7]. Deleted the pre-IPO wording and the Rp1,600bn split from the assumptions basis, the fact label, section 3 and section 6, and kept the governance point on the controller's 90% share of the post-IPO distributions [S11].

challenges.challenge: Effective 1 January 2026 the company extended machinery and building lives from 8 and 20 years to 30 years, cutting 9M26 depreciation by Rp74.49bn: total depreciation fell to Rp40.5bn (COGS Rp37.9bn, G&A Rp2.6bn) from Rp116.5bn in 9M25, about 1.8% of revenue. The model holds D&A at 5.0% of revenue to FY2035, so FY2026E net profit of Rp524.7bn is understated by roughly Rp72bn (EPS about Rp69.8, not Rp61.4) and the implied Q4 2026E profit of Rp75.5bn is 46% below Q4 2025's Rp140.2bn on no operational driver. The earnings-quality screens never mention the estimate change.
challenges.answer: Accepted and corrected: the template EBIT is struck after depreciation because its gross margin and SG&A ratios are the reported ones, which include the charge inside COGS and G&A, so the life extension lifts EBIT as well as cutting the D&A add-back - section 3 now says exactly that. D&A is rebuilt on the post-1 January 2026 lives at 1.95% of revenue in FY2026E rising to 2.25%, from the nine-month charge of Rp41.58bn cut by Rp74.49bn and the Rp454.59bn of fully depreciated assets; FY2026E EPS is 68.4 and FY2027E 71.1 [S6]. The change is an optics-class disclosed flag in section 3 with its Rp74.49bn nine-month effect [S6][S7].

challenges.challenge: The engine's gross margin is 36.89% in FY2026E fading to 34.07% by FY2035E (the corn link charges 3.3% of COGS on a 172.6 to 214.6 deck move at 30% COGS share and 45% absorption), but §3, §4 and §7 all tell the reader 38.9% fading to 37.5%, and §7 sets the monitoring KPI against 38.9%. The stated primary value driver is not the modelled one.
challenges.answer: The text now quotes the modelled line, not the input: printed gross margin 39.2% in FY2026E (the nine-month actual), 37.5% by FY2030E and 36.2% by FY2035E, and the section 7 KPI is set on fin.FY2026E.gross_margin [S6]. The inputs were rebased using the house MYOR convention so the margin the model prints is the margin we intend, after the corn link lifts COGS by about 3.3% [S0].

challenges.challenge: The calibration gate shows a -2.2pp EBITDA-margin drift (FY2026E 29.2% vs FY2025A 31.4%) with no qc_justification recorded. Its only driver is the corn series rising 24% in FY2026, while the actual accounts show the opposite: 9M26 gross margin 39.2% against 33.2% a year earlier because raw materials fell faster than net revenue. §2 also says the deck does not assume costs fall further when the deck assumes a 24% rise.
challenges.answer: qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin rewritten: the 2.7pp EBITDA-margin gap is the nine-month 2026 cost base, not a haircut and not the depreciation change. In 9M26 operating profit of Rp599.56bn plus depreciation of Rp41.58bn on revenue of Rp2,237.26bn is a 28.7% margin, and FY2026E is 28.8%; SG&A net of other operating income ran at 12.36% of revenue against 6.7% a year earlier, with marketing and promotion at Rp62.86bn against Rp33.00bn, and at constant depreciation that step exceeds the gross-profit gain [S6]. EBITDA is struck before depreciation, so the life extension only lifts EBIT and cuts the add-back by the same amount. Section 2 now says the deck holds corn about a quarter above its FY2025 average rather than rising through FY2029 [S0], and the FY2026E operating-cost input is set at the nine-month actual of 12.36% rather than above it [S6].

challenges.challenge: FY2026 dividends already declared are Rp141.6bn + Rp145.4bn + Rp126.75bn = Rp413.8bn, which is 78.9% of FY2026E net profit of Rp524.7bn, not about 70%. The model pays 70% (DPS Rp42.99) against Rp48.42 a share already declared, and forecast dividends_paid uses lagged FY2025 DPS (Rp287.0bn), so FY2026E cash outflow is Rp126.8bn below the declared run-rate.
